# Comparing the worlds

> *A drug that cures a bacterial pneumonia does nothing for influenza, and a blood film that shows
> malaria parasites shows no viruses. The six questions have different answers for bacteria, viruses,
> fungi and parasites, and those answers explain why each kind of microbe is detected, treated and
> prevented in its own way.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Compare bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and helminths on each of the six questions, with an
  anchor organism for each.
- Explain why antibacterial drugs do not treat viral infection, and why antifungal and antiparasitic
  drugs are fewer, and some of them more toxic, than antibacterial drugs.
- Relate the reservoir and route of an infection to whether it is prevented mainly by vaccination,
  vector control, sanitation or screening.
- Compare latency, chronic infection and autoinfection as ways in which organisms from different
  worlds persist in the host.
- Match each kind of microbe to the laboratory methods that can find it, and explain the match from
  its structure and growth.
- Decide the most likely kind of microbe from a patient's story, and use the six questions to make
  predictions about an organism not met before.
:::

## Six questions, five answers {#sec-cmp-questions}

### The comparison {#sec-cmp-table}

The six questions apply to every kind of microbe (see [*The microbial
world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-six)), and each world answers them in its own
way. The answers for each world, with its anchor organism (see [*The microbial
world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-anchors)), are:

| Question | Bacteria (*Staphylococcus aureus*) | Viruses (influenza virus) | Fungi (*Candida albicans*) | Protozoa (*Plasmodium falciparum*) | Helminths (*Ascaris lumbricoides*) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| What is it built from? | A prokaryotic cell: no nucleus, 70S ribosomes, usually a peptidoglycan wall | Not a cell: a DNA or RNA genome in a protein capsid, sometimes inside a lipid envelope | A eukaryotic cell with a chitin and glucan wall and ergosterol in its membrane | A single eukaryotic cell with no cell wall in its active form; many intestinal protozoa form walled cysts that survive outside the host | A many-celled animal with tissues and organs |
| How does it get energy, and what does it need to grow? | Its own metabolism; needs for oxygen range from obligate aerobe to obligate anaerobe | None of its own: it uses the host cell's ribosomes, energy and building blocks | Its own metabolism, absorbing nutrients; many fungi grow poorly at 37 °C | Its own metabolism, using nutrients from host cells, blood or gut contents | Its own metabolism, using gut contents, blood or tissue |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Binary fission; mutation and gene transfer between cells | Assembled from parts made inside a host cell; RNA viruses mutate rapidly, and segmented genomes reassort | Budding in yeasts, spores in moulds; mutation | Repeated division inside the host; some reproduce sexually in a mosquito or other host | Sexual reproduction; eggs or larvae leave the host, and with few exceptions the worms do not multiply inside it |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | Body surfaces, soil, water and food; by contact, air, food, water and arthropods | Multiplies only inside host cells; spreads by respiratory particles, the faecal–oral route, blood and sexual contact, or arthropods | The person's own microbiota, or soil and decaying matter from which spores are inhaled; dermatophytes spread by contact with people and animals, and few other fungi pass from person to person | Blood, gut, tissues or genital tract; by the bite of mosquitoes and other arthropods, cysts in food or water, sexual contact, or across the placenta | Intestine and tissues; eggs or larvae in soil, water or meat, swallowed or entering through the skin |
| How does damage happen? | Invasion, toxins and the host response ([*How bacteria cause damage*](../bacteria/bacterial-damage.qmd#sec-bdam-source)) | Death of infected cells, the immune response to them, loss of the cells infected, and in some cases cancer ([*Viruses and the host*](../viruses/virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-damage)) | Invasion when a defence fails; allergy; toxins in food ([*Fungal principles*](../fungi/fungal-principles.qmd#sec-fun-damage)) | Destruction of the cells it lives in, blockage of small vessels, and the host response ([*Protozoa*](../parasites/protozoa.qmd#sec-proto-falciparum)) | Mostly in proportion to the number of worms in the intestine (obstruction, loss of blood and nutrients); larvae or eggs lodged in tissue harm mainly through the host response ([*Helminths*](../parasites/helminths.qmd#sec-helm-burden)) |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | Peptidoglycan, 70S ribosomes and many bacterial enzymes | A few viral enzymes and other proteins, such as RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and reverse transcriptase | Ergosterol and the chitin and glucan wall | A few parasite pathways, such as the folate synthesis of *P. falciparum* | Worm nerve and muscle ion channels; worm tubulin |
| Opening chapter | [*How bacteria are built and get energy*](../bacteria/bacteria-build-energy.qmd) | [*How viruses are built and copy themselves*](../viruses/virus-structure-replication.qmd) | [*Fungal principles*](../fungi/fungal-principles.qmd) | [*Life cycles and vectors*](../parasites/life-cycles.qmd) | [*Life cycles and vectors*](../parasites/life-cycles.qmd) |

### Three dividing lines {#sec-cmp-lines}

Three of the answers divide the worlds most sharply, and most of the practical differences between
them follow from these three:

- Whether the agent is a cell. A virus has no ribosomes and makes no energy, so it is copied only
  inside a living cell, is too small for the light microscope, and offers drugs only the few enzymes
  and other proteins it encodes (see [*How viruses are built and copy
  themselves*](../viruses/virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-structure)).
- Whether the cell is a prokaryote or a eukaryote. A bacterium differs from a human cell in its wall,
  its ribosomes and many of its enzymes, whereas fungi, protozoa and helminths share most of their
  machinery with human cells (see [*The microbial
  world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-kinds)).
- Whether the organism multiplies inside the human host. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa do, so
  a small inoculum, the number of organisms received, can become a large infection; most helminths
  do not, so the number of worms follows the number of eggs or larvae that entered (see [*Life
  cycles and vectors*](../parasites/life-cycles.qmd#sec-life-kinds)).

The fourth question, where an organism lives and how it spreads, divides the worlds far less. Each
route of transmission carries organisms from several worlds, which is why the route decides how an
infection is prevented more than the kind of microbe does ([Prevention](#sec-cmp-prevent)).

::: {.callout-important}
## Is a virus a very small bacterium?
Viruses and bacteria are often pictured as smaller and larger versions of the same thing, because
both are invisible to the eye and both cause fevers, coughs and diarrhoea that can look alike. A
virus differs from a bacterium in what it is built from, how it gets energy and how it is copied: it
is not a cell, has no ribosomes and makes no energy, and it is copied only inside a host cell, so it
does not grow on agar (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](../viruses/virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-cycle)).
:::

## What the differences predict {#sec-cmp-predict}

### Drugs: what each kind has that human cells lack {#sec-cmp-drugs}

Every antimicrobial drug depends on **selective toxicity**: harming a microbe without harming the
host, by acting on something the microbe has and the host lacks (see [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](../bacteria/bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-glance)). The safe targets become fewer as a
microbe's machinery comes closer to that of human cells, or, for a virus, as more of its work is done
by the host cell itself:

| Kind of microbe | What it shares with human cells | What drugs act on | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bacteria | The genetic code and the basic chemistry of energy | The peptidoglycan wall, 70S ribosomes and bacterial enzymes | Many classes of drug, several of them active against many species |
| Viruses | Everything it uses to make proteins and energy, which belongs to the host cell | A few viral enzymes and proteins | Few drugs, most of them for one virus or one family; none acts on a viral genome lying silent in a cell |
| Fungi | Nucleus, mitochondria, 80S ribosomes and enzymes much like human ones | Ergosterol and the wall | Few classes; the polyenes also bind cholesterol and damage the kidney |
| Protozoa | The machinery of a eukaryotic cell | A few pathways, such as the folate synthesis and haem disposal of *P. falciparum* | Few drugs, each for particular parasites |
| Helminths | Animal tissues, including nerves and muscles | Worm nerve and muscle ion channels; worm tubulin | Drugs that paralyse intestinal worms, so that they are expelled, or that bind worm tubulin |

Antibacterial drugs do not treat viral infection. A virus has no wall, and its proteins are made on
the host cell's 80S ribosomes, so drugs aimed at peptidoglycan or the 70S ribosome have nothing in it
to act on (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](../viruses/virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-targets)). In a viral illness these
drugs still act on the resident bacteria, so they add side effects without shortening the illness,
and every course selects resistant bacteria (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](../bacteria/bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-stewardship)). They help only when a bacterial
infection follows, as bacterial pneumonia can follow influenza (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
targets*](../viruses/detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-few)).

::: {.example}
An antibacterial drug taken for influenza leaves the virus untouched, but it can reduce the vaginal
bacteria and let *C. albicans*, which the drug spares, overgrow in their place (see [*Fungal
principles*](../fungi/fungal-principles.qmd#sec-fun-defences)).
:::

Antifungal and antiparasitic drugs are fewer than antibacterial drugs, and some of them harm the
patient more. Fungi, protozoa and helminths are eukaryotes, and most drugs that blocked their
ribosomes, their DNA copying or their energy supply would block the patient's as well, so the drugs
in use act on the few differences (see [*Fungal
principles*](../fungi/fungal-principles.qmd#sec-fun-few) and [*Life cycles and vectors*](../parasites/life-cycles.qmd#sec-life-targets)). Where a difference is
only one of degree, the drug also harms human cells: the polyenes bind ergosterol, but they also bind
cholesterol. Where the target has no human counterpart, or the parasite's version binds the drug far
more tightly than the human one, the drug can be well tolerated. The echinocandins act on the fungal
wall and cause few side effects, and drugs that bind worm tubulin are safe enough to give to whole
populations of school-age children (see [*Life cycles and
vectors*](../parasites/life-cycles.qmd#sec-life-control)).

Resistance arises in every world by mutation and selection, and bacteria also acquire it by gene
transfer (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](../bacteria/bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-hgt)). HIV infection, tuberculosis and falciparum
malaria, infections from three worlds, are all treated with **combination therapy**: treatment with
two or more drugs acting on different targets, so that a variant resistant to one is still suppressed
by the others (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
targets*](../viruses/detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-resistance)). In each, the organism's population
in an untreated patient is large enough that variants resistant to a single drug are likely to be
present, or to arise during treatment, and a single drug would select them. Treatment of
tuberculosis also lasts months, because *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* grows slowly and some of the
bacteria divide slowly or barely at all, so drugs kill them only slowly (see [*Atypicals and
mycobacteria*](../bacteria/atypicals-mycobacteria.qmd#sec-atyp-tuberculosis)).

### Prevention {#sec-cmp-prevent}

Prevention acts on a link in the chain of infection (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-chain)). The link chosen depends on
where the organism lives between hosts and how it travels, more than on its kind:

| What the infection depends on | Main prevention | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Spread from person to person, with immunity after recovery | A vaccine | Influenza virus, with a vaccine updated each year as the virus changes |
| A **vector**, an arthropod that carries an organism between hosts | Vector control: bed nets treated with insecticide, insecticide sprayed in homes, removing water in which mosquitoes breed | *P. falciparum*, carried by *Anopheles* mosquitoes; dengue virus, carried by *Aedes* mosquitoes ([*Arthropod-borne viruses*](../viruses/arboviruses.qmd#sec-arbo-dengue)) |
| Faeces reaching food, water, soil or hands | Sanitation, safe water, and washing hands and food | *A. lumbricoides*; *Giardia duodenalis*; norovirus |
| A silent infection that lasts for years, carried in blood and genital fluids | Testing of blood donations, pregnant women and people at risk; treatment of those found infected, which also stops sexual spread once the virus is suppressed; condoms; drugs taken before exposure by people at risk; and safe needles | HIV ([*Blood-borne and sexually transmitted viruses*](../viruses/bloodborne-viruses.qmd#sec-bbv-hiv)) |
| The person's own microbiota | Protecting barriers and the microbiota: care of catheters and wounds, and sparing use of antibacterial drugs | *S. aureus*; *C. albicans* |
| Soil or water, with no spread between people | Avoiding exposure, especially for people with a host factor such as diabetes | *Burkholderia pseudomallei* |

**Vaccination**, making a host immune without causing disease by giving a vaccine, is in routine use
against many viruses and bacteria. No vaccine is in routine use against a fungus or a helminth, and
the malaria vaccines given to young children in parts of Africa give partial protection (see [*Life
cycles and vectors*](../parasites/life-cycles.qmd#sec-life-control)). The organisms with no
vaccine, or only a partial one, each show a difficulty:

- The body almost never clears HIV infection, so there is no recovery whose protection a vaccine
  could copy, and the virus varies widely within and between people (see [*How viruses
  change*](../viruses/virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-vaccines)).
- Partial immunity to *P. falciparum* builds up only after years of repeated infection, and it fades
  when exposure stops (see [*Protozoa*](../parasites/protozoa.qmd#sec-proto-falciparum)).
- Invasive fungal infection occurs mainly in people whose defences have already failed, as in
  advanced HIV infection, in which the CD4 T cells that a response to a vaccine depends on are lost
  (see [*Fungal principles*](../fungi/fungal-principles.qmd#sec-fun-defences)).
- People who live where worms are common are infected again and again throughout life, and the number
  of worms is kept low instead by sanitation and regular treatment (see
  [*Helminths*](../parasites/helminths.qmd#sec-helm-burden)).

The route also decides who a vaccine protects. Against an organism passed from person to person,
vaccinating enough people protects the unvaccinated as well (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-measures)). Against an organism caught
only from soil or water, a vaccine would protect only the person who receives it (see [*Detecting and
controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-prevent)).

### Persistence {#sec-cmp-persist}

Organisms from every world can stay in the body for years after they arrive. Two of the ways they do
so are the time courses described for every infection (see
[*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-courses)): **latent
infection**, the persistence of an organism in a silent state, with the possibility of reactivation,
and **chronic infection**, in which infection and inflammation continue for months or years. A third
is seen in only a few worms, most importantly *Strongyloides stercoralis*: **autoinfection**, the
reinfection of a host by larvae that mature inside it.

| Way of persisting | What persists, and where | What follows | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carriage in the microbiota | A living population on a body surface, causing no disease | Infection comes from the person's own organisms when a barrier is breached, defences fail or the microbiota is disturbed | *S. aureus* in the nose; *C. albicans* in the gut and vagina |
| Latency | A silent form that multiplies little or not at all: a viral genome in nerve cells, or bacteria walled into granulomas | Reactivation years later, often when the defences that held it in check fail; drugs cannot clear a latent virus, but latent *M. tuberculosis* can be treated | Herpes simplex virus in sensory nerve cells ([*Viruses and the host*](../viruses/virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-latency)); *M. tuberculosis* in the lung |
| Chronic infection | Continuous multiplication despite an immune response | Damage builds up over years, and the person can transmit the organism throughout, often without knowing | HIV, which also persists as DNA integrated into the chromosomes of resting CD4 T cells ([*Viruses and the host*](../viruses/virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-chronic)) |
| Autoinfection | Larvae that mature in the gut and reinfect the same person | Infection decades after the person left the place where it was caught; overwhelming infection when drugs suppress the defences | *S. stercoralis* ([*Helminths*](../parasites/helminths.qmd#sec-helm-strongyloides)) |
| Dormant liver stages | Parasites resting inside liver cells | Relapse of malaria months, and occasionally years, after the first illness; drugs that clear the blood stages leave them untouched | *Plasmodium vivax* and *Plasmodium ovale*; *P. falciparum* forms no dormant liver stage |

Several of these organisms are held in check by **cell-mediated immunity**, the defence by T cells
against infected cells and against organisms that live inside host cells. When it fails, as CD4 T
cells are lost in advanced HIV infection, latent *M. tuberculosis* and herpesviruses reactivate (see
[*Viruses and the host*](../viruses/virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-cd4)). **Corticosteroids**, drugs that
suppress inflammation and immune responses, let the larvae of *S. stercoralis* multiply (see
[*Helminths*](../parasites/helminths.qmd#sec-helm-strongyloides)). A persistent infection that causes
no symptoms is therefore looked for before such defences are suppressed.

::: {.example}
Before treatment with drugs that suppress immunity, such as high-dose corticosteroids or the drugs
given after a transplant, patients are often tested for latent *M. tuberculosis*, for hepatitis B
virus and, if they have lived where the worm is common, for *S. stercoralis*, so that those found
infected can be treated before the infection flares.
:::

### Detection {#sec-cmp-detect}

Microscopy and culture read an organism's structure and growth, which differ most between the
worlds. A **nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)**, a test that copies a target sequence many times
until it can be detected, and **serology**, the detection of a patient's antibodies as evidence of
exposure, work in the same way for every kind of microbe (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-kinds)).

| Kind of microbe | Seen with a light microscope? | Grown in the laboratory? | Usual first tests | Anchor example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bacteria | Yes, after staining: the Gram stain, or the acid-fast stain for mycobacteria; a few, such as *Mycoplasma* and *Chlamydia*, are not seen on a Gram stain | Most grow on agar overnight; *M. tuberculosis* takes weeks, and some bacteria cannot be grown on agar at all | Gram stain and culture of a sample from the site; NAATs for bacteria that grow slowly or not at all ([*Detecting bacteria and testing susceptibility*](../bacteria/detecting-bacteria.qmd)) | *S. aureus*: purple cocci in clusters on a Gram stain of pus, and colonies the next day |
| Viruses | Not as virions: most are smaller than the light microscope can resolve, though the changes a virus causes in infected cells can sometimes be seen | Only inside living cells, mainly in reference laboratories | NAATs, antigen tests and serology ([*Detecting viruses and antiviral targets*](../viruses/detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-methods)) | Influenza virus: a NAAT on a swab from the nose or throat |
| Fungi | Yes: yeast cells and hyphae | Most, from a day or two for yeasts to weeks for some moulds; *Pneumocystis jirovecii* does not grow in routine culture | Microscopy and culture; antigen tests in blood or cerebrospinal fluid, the fluid around the brain and spinal cord ([*Fungal principles*](../fungi/fungal-principles.qmd#sec-fun-methods)) | *C. albicans*: budding cells several times the size of a bacterium on a Gram stain |
| Protozoa | Yes, in blood or stool | Rarely used for diagnosis | Microscopy of a blood film or a stool sample; antigen tests ([*Life cycles and vectors*](../parasites/life-cycles.qmd#sec-life-detect)) | *P. falciparum*: parasites inside red cells on a stained blood film |
| Helminths | Eggs and larvae under the microscope; most adult worms by eye | Rarely used for diagnosis | Microscopy of stool for eggs or larvae; serology for larvae hidden in tissue ([*Helminths*](../parasites/helminths.qmd#sec-helm-sentence)) | *A. lumbricoides*: eggs in the stool |

The kind of microbe suspected therefore decides which sample is taken and which test is asked for. A
Gram stain cannot show a virus, and a blood culture cannot grow *P. falciparum*. Serology finds its
place in every world where the organism is out of reach of a sample, or persists alongside the
antibodies, as HIV does.

::: {.example}
By the time a liver abscess caused by the protozoan *Entamoeba histolytica* appears, the stool often
contains no parasites, so the laboratory looks for antibodies against it (see
[*Protozoa*](../parasites/protozoa.qmd#sec-proto-entamoeba)).
:::

## Deciding the kind of microbe {#sec-cmp-kind}

In a patient's story, some clues separate the kinds of microbe and others cut across them. Clues
that come from what an organism is built from, how it grows and what drugs act on it separate the
worlds, because these are the answers that differ most between them:

| Clue | Points towards | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Cells seen on a Gram stain, and colonies on agar within a day or two | A bacterium, or a yeast | Both are cells large enough to stain, with their own metabolism; yeast cells are several times larger than bacteria and bud |
| A positive NAAT, with nothing seen on a stain and nothing grown on agar | A virus, or a bacterium that cannot be grown on agar | Viruses are too small for the light microscope and multiply only inside living cells |
| Parasites inside red cells on a blood film | A protozoan | *P. falciparum* multiplies inside red cells |
| Eggs or larvae in the stool | A helminth | Adult worms in the intestine, or in the bile ducts or the veins of the intestine, release eggs or larvae that reach the stool; the intestinal protozoa pass cysts |
| **Eosinophilia**, a raised count of eosinophils in the blood | Among infections, a helminth moving through tissue | **Eosinophils** are white blood cells that attack parasites too large to engulf |
| An illness that does not respond to an antibacterial drug | A virus, a fungus or a parasite, or a bacterium resistant to that drug | Antibacterial drugs act only on bacterial structures |

Clues from the route and from the host narrow the list, but they cut across the worlds:

- A mosquito bite can carry a protozoan, *P. falciparum*, or a virus, such as dengue virus.
- Food or water contaminated with faeces carries viruses, bacteria, protozoa and helminths.
- Failing cell-mediated immunity in advanced HIV infection lets organisms from four worlds cause
  disease: *M. tuberculosis*, herpesviruses, *Cryptococcus neoformans* and *Toxoplasma gondii* among
  them.
- **Neutropenia**, an abnormally low neutrophil count, lets both bacteria and fungi through.

A route or a host factor therefore gives a short list of organisms, often from several worlds, and a
laboratory finding or the response to treatment then decides between them.

::: {.example}
A traveller with fever after a stay in an area where both malaria and dengue occur could have either
infection; parasites inside red cells on a blood film place the cause among the protozoa.
:::

Sort each description below by the kind of microbe it describes. None of them names the organism.

## Reasoning about an unfamiliar organism {#sec-cmp-unfamiliar}

The six questions apply equally to an organism met for the first time, in a report from another
country or in a patient who has travelled. The first answer, the kind of microbe, brings with it
answers to the other five, each a prediction that can be checked. *Angiostrongylus cantonensis*, the
rat lungworm, is one such organism.

::: {.example}
*A. cantonensis* is a roundworm found in South-East Asia and the Pacific islands, among other places.
The adult worms live in the arteries of the lungs of rats, and their larvae pass out in rat faeces
and develop in snails and slugs, which rats eat. People are infected by eating raw or undercooked
snails or slugs, or vegetables contaminated with them, and also by eating raw freshwater prawns, crabs
or frogs that carry larvae from snails they have eaten. In a person, the larvae travel to the brain
and its meninges and die there without completing the life cycle.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Predict: will a stool sample from an infected person show eggs? (Click to check)
No. The larvae never become egg-laying adults in a person, and they lodge in the brain, not the gut,
so nothing reaches the stool. The roundworm *Toxocara*, whose larvae wander through human tissues
without maturing, gives the same negative stool sample (see
[*Helminths*](../parasites/helminths.qmd#sec-helm-supporting)).
:::

For *A. cantonensis*, the **definitive host**, the host in which a parasite reproduces sexually, is
the rat, and the **intermediate hosts**, hosts in which a parasite develops or multiplies without
reproducing sexually, are snails and slugs (see [*Life cycles and
vectors*](../parasites/life-cycles.qmd#sec-life-vectors)). A person is a **dead-end host**, a host
from which an organism is not passed on, as people are for Japanese encephalitis virus (see
[*Arthropod-borne viruses*](../viruses/arboviruses.qmd#sec-arbo-supporting)).

| Question | What the description gives | What can be predicted |
|---|---|---|
| What is it built from? | A roundworm: a many-celled animal | Far too large for a phagocyte to engulf, so eosinophils are likely to gather around the larvae and to appear in the cerebrospinal fluid |
| How does it get energy? | Its own metabolism, as for every helminth | Nothing beyond what holds for every helminth |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Adults reproduce in rats; in a person the larvae do not complete the life cycle | No multiplication in a person, so the number of larvae, and probably the severity, depends on how many were swallowed; no eggs in the stool, and no spread from one person to another |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | Rats are the definitive host and snails and slugs the intermediate hosts; people are infected by eating snails or slugs, or animals that have eaten them | Caught from raw or undercooked snails, slugs, freshwater prawns, crabs or frogs, or unwashed vegetables, so cooking and washing food prevent it; the reservoir is in animals, so it cannot be eradicated, and its control is a One Health problem ([*Transmission, outbreaks and One Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-onehealth)) |
| How does damage happen? | Larvae in the brain and its meninges | **Meningitis**, inflammation of the meninges, the membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord; much of the damage from the host's response to the larvae, as with other helminth larvae lodged in tissue ([*Helminths*](../parasites/helminths.qmd#sec-helm-burden)) |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | Worm nerve and muscle ion channels; worm tubulin | Drugs that act on worms exist ([*Life cycles and vectors*](../parasites/life-cycles.qmd#sec-life-targets)); killing larvae in the brain might add to the inflammation around them, so whether such a drug helps is a question for clinical studies |

As predicted, the cerebrospinal fluid of people infected with *A. cantonensis* contains many
eosinophils, and the illness is known as eosinophilic meningitis.
